passage: Amandeep stepped onto the balcony of his Pune flat at eleven, lit a cigarette and felt his shoulders drop for the first time since the audit call. The traffic below hummed. For a few minutes the knot in his chest loosened. By one in the morning it was back, tighter, and he went out for another. Then another. Next morning his flatmate Rajni counted the stubs in the saucer and raised an eyebrow. "Rough week?" she asked. Amandeep looked at the saucer too. Four months ago it had been one on Fridays. Now the calm lasted less and the jitters came sooner. That evening, when the worry rose again, he left the packet in a drawer, walked two rounds of the colony with Rajni and told her about the audit. He also booked a chat with the company counsellor for Monday.

qa.a: He stepped onto the balcony of his Pune flat.

qa.a: He felt uneasy, even a little alarmed, because he could see the calm was lasting less while the jitters came sooner than four months ago.

qa.q: What turning point in the evening helped Amandeep, and why?
qa.a: Leaving the packet in a drawer, walking with Rajni and booking the counsellor gave him other supports for the worry, before the habit grew stronger.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel seeing the stubs pile up?
qa.a: Rajni probably felt concerned but did not want to lecture, so she asked a gentle question and later joined him on the walk.

"Third night this week, Tanvir," Himani said, nodding at the glass as she packed her bag at the co-working space.
"It's just to switch my head off. The launch is killing me."
"Does it switch off?"
"For an hour. Then I wake at four with my heart racing, thinking about the launch anyway."
"And the next night you need two."
Tanvir laughed, then stopped. "Yeah. Actually, yeah."
"My cousin went down that road. It crept up slowly."
"I'm not... I just don't know what else calms me down."
"What used to?"
"Football. Cooking. Calling my brother."
"When did you last do any of that?"
He was quiet. "Before the launch."
"There's a five-a-side on Thursdays near the metro. Come."
"Okay. And maybe I'll mention the four a.m. thing to my doctor."
"Good. I'll hold you to Thursday."

qa.a: He wakes at four with his heart racing.

qa.a: He felt caught off guard and uneasy, laughing first and then admitting it was true.

qa.q: What would you advise Tanvir now that he has seen the pattern?
qa.a: Go back to things that calmed him before, like football and calling his brother, and tell his doctor about waking at four with a racing heart.

qa.q: What is it like for Himani to raise this with Tanvir?
qa.a: It is probably awkward for Himani, but because her cousin slid slowly, she cares enough to ask and offers something to do instead.

Supervisor's note, audit team, Friday
When Francis joined in June, he took one smoke break after lunch. Since the year-end audit began, I've watched it grow to five or six a day. He comes back calmer for a few minutes, then is jittery again within the hour, tapping his pen and checking his pocket. Today he admitted, 'It's the only thing that switches my brain off. Then the worry comes back worse.' I spoke to him privately and without judgement. I told him that pattern of quick relief and bounce-back sounded exhausting, and that noticing it early was good. We agreed he could take walking breaks with me after lunch instead, and I gave him the details of the company counsellor and the doctor's clinic. He booked the counsellor for Tuesday.
Rashmi, audit manager

qa.a: One smoke break after lunch.

qa.a: He feels calmer for a few minutes, then jittery and worried again, with the anxiety coming back worse.

qa.a: Rashmi spoke privately without judgement, offered walking breaks instead and shared details of the counsellor and doctor.

qa.a: It may feel uncomfortable at first, but also a relief to have someone understand why he keeps going back.

passage:
Thursday, 3 am
Awake again. This is the fourth night this week. Writing so I stop pretending.
Since the new job, I've been pouring a glass of wine every evening 'to switch off'. Then it became two. For an hour I feel loose and fine. Then I wake at three with my heart pounding, thinking about every email I didn't answer. Tonight I realised: the wine isn't stopping the worry. It's lending me a few hours of quiet and charging interest. And I've started wanting it by four in the afternoon, which scares me.
I'm going to tell Mahima tomorrow. She'll be kind. No wine on weeknights for now. Walk after work instead, and call Mahima when it's bad. If it's hard to stop, I'll see the doctor.
Amandeep

qa.a: Four nights.

passage: Every evening after the last bus left the Chandpur stand, Vidya walked behind the grain shop and lit a cigarette. It had started in March, when the school inspection was coming and her mother's knee was getting worse. The first drag loosened her shoulders for a few minutes. Then, an hour later, her chest felt tight, the worry came back louder, and she wanted another. By June she was planning her whole day around that back wall. One evening Deepika, who ran the tailoring shop next door, found her there with shaking fingers. "Is it helping?" Deepika asked. Vidya laughed, then didn't. On Monday they took the bus together to the district health centre, and Vidya asked the doctor what help there was to stop.

qa.q: Where does Vidya go to smoke every evening?
qa.a: She goes behind the grain shop after the last bus leaves the Chandpur stand.

qa.q: What did Vidya feel an hour after smoking, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt anxious again, even more than before; her chest was tight, the worry came back louder and she wanted another.

qa.q: What turning point shows Vidya noticing the pattern, and what did she do about it?
qa.a: She saw she was planning her day around the back wall, and after Deepika's question she went to the district health centre to ask for help to stop.

qa.q: How might Deepika have felt finding Vidya with shaking fingers?
qa.a: Deepika was probably concerned, and chose a gentle question instead of a lecture.
